newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasury scraps two 10-year note sales.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury scraps two 10-year note sales.

text.p: A plunging government budget deficit and popular new debt products have enabled the Treasury to scrap sales of some securities and to offer new inflation-protected ones, Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said on Monday.
Summers told a news conference that the Treasury was dropping sales of conventional, fixed-rate 10-year notes in July and October -- cutting sales back to four times a year from six.
In addition, the Treasury is broadening its offerings of a new type of inflation-protected securities to include one with a five-year maturity that will be auctioned in July and October.

Summers said the new five-year, inflation-protected security builds upon the success of a 10-year indexed note introduced last January and will be one in a series of the securities carrying varied maturities and offering investors protection against the ravages of inflation.
The Treasury sold $7 billion of the 10-year indexed notes in January and another $8 billion in May but it will not offer any more of this maturity this year.
"We have been pleased with the market response (to the 10-year indexed notes)," Summers said, adding: "A liquid market has developed."
He said that five mutual-fund companies were now selling products that were based on the 10-year indexed notes and added that insurance companies and pension funds were interested in them.
A new 10-year indexed note will be sold next January, Summers said. Sometime next year, the Treasury also will begin offering inflation-indexed bonds with a 30-year maturity.
"By the end of next year, we expect to establish a regular schedule for offering inflation-indexed securities with maturities of five, 10 and 30 years," Summers said.

The indexed securities adjust the interest that investors receive according to changes in the widely used consumer price index, in contrast to conventional securities that offer a set interest rate that is determined at the time they are sold.
Thus, a buyer of indexed securities has greater certainty that his earnings will not be eroded by rising prices by the time the security matures.

Summers said that over time the Treasury expects to increase the proportion of government debt issued in the form of inflation-protected securities to "a substantial fraction" but would not be specific.
He also declined to say how frequently sales of five-, 10- and 30-year indexed securities will occur. "We'll have to see," he said in response to questions.
Summers repeated, in response to questions, that the Treasury plans to also offer an inflation-protected U.S. Savings Bond early next year.

Some analysts have said the inflation-protected securities might be less attractive to investors because inflation, measured by the consumer price index compiled by the government, has been low and stable so that the chances of a higher return than on a conventional security were reduced.

Summers acknowledged that inflation was remaining under control but nonetheless extolled the benefits of the new securities, saying the reason they have proven "less volatile" than conventional securities was partly because of changed inflation expectations.

The government's spending deficit is expected to fall below $100 billion in the current financial year ending Sept. 30. A flood of tax revenues into the Treasury's coffers from the expanding economy and from a booming stock market has shrunk the shortfall between spending and income and thus reduced borrowing needs.
Summers was noncommital when asked whether the Treasury might be able to scrap more sales of conventional 10-year notes in addition to the two sales that it is dropping in July and October.
